structure.title: 4.3 to 4.6 Engagement after treatment, sanctions, over time, event study
Appendices A to C (timeline, disclosure examples, variable definitions)

observations.statement: The identifying assumption is stated as local randomness of treatment around a proxy-advisor policy threshold on the say-on-pay vote share, framed as a quasi-natural experiment; the design is named a sharp RD complemented by ATE regressions and difference-in-differences.
observations.quote: our identifying assumption is that whether a firm receives ISS treatment is locally random

observations.statement: Before validating the cutoff, the authors ask whether the same threshold matters to other constituents (the second proxy advisor, large asset managers) and argue those thresholds differ or lack a stated policy, with a Big-3 ownership check delegated to the Internet Appendix.

The ATE regression is presented with two named assumptions, parallel trends (tested later via event-time indicators) and SUTVA; spillovers to control firms are argued to bias toward underestimating the effect.

Hypotheses are numbered (H1 to H4b) and derived from institutional theory before any data are shown; one hypothesis is stated in null form because competing predictions exist, and forces that could obscure evidence are listed.
The authors report verifying their interpretation of the advisor's policy directly with the institution and cite conversations for how the policy originated.

The full sample is all say-on-pay votes in ISS Voting Analytics over a stated multi-year window, matched to proxy statements on the SEC site and merged with CRSP and Compustat; the unit is the firm-year and the sample sizes are stated in the text.

The RD subsample keeps only firms that fall within a narrow window around the threshold for the first time in the sample period, and drops observations with missing controls; the narrow window is justified for clean testing with wider bandwidths as robustness.
Sample completeness is cross-verified against a list of below-threshold firms supplied directly by the proxy advisor.

Glass Lewis recommendations for a subsample are obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request to a state pension system, following a prior paper; limited coverage is given as a reason not to use them in main specifications.
Every regression table reports the number of firms or firm-years; RD and balance tables report treated and control counts separately for each bandwidth or variable.

Outcomes are built by a Python script that flags engagement keywords within a fixed character distance of shareholder keywords in proxy statements; an indicator captures the extensive margin and a keyword count the intensive margin.

Because some disclosures are in images the script cannot read, the RD subsample is hand-checked; script-only results are moved to the Internet Appendix. Depth and breadth measures are hand-collected from a uniform random draw of proxy statements.

The running variable follows the advisor's own definition of vote support (for divided by for plus against, abstentions excluded); treatment is an indicator for support in a narrow band just below the cutoff, control just above.
Coding of missing breadth measures is made explicit: set to zero when no engagement is disclosed, treated as missing when engagement is disclosed without percentages.

CEO pay and analyst counts enter in logs (one plus count for analysts); for RD on the count outcome, log of one plus the count is used to handle skew from zeros, whereas the ATE regressions use Poisson on the raw count.
All variables are defined in a dedicated appendix table, and every table note points to it.

Regression tables carry rows naming the estimator (OLS or Poisson), which FE are included, controls yes/no, N and adjusted or pseudo R2; t-statistics in parentheses; clustering is described in the notes.
A linear probability model is chosen over probit or logit to avoid FE bias, with a citation; Poisson is used for count outcomes citing a finance methods paper.

Controls for the treatment regressions are chosen from the determinants analysis; variables lacking significance there are dropped citing an overcontrol concern, and the authors state results are insensitive to that choice.

The sharp RD omits covariates and FE, justified by the balance table; the text states the estimator (robust bias-corrected), the kernel (triangular), the polynomial order (local linear, quadratic as robustness citing the high-order polynomial critique) and the bandwidth choices.
A summary panel above the treatment regressions gives mean, median and SD for treated and control firms plus the pooled mean, which is then used as the base for interpreting coefficients.

Standard errors are two-way clustered (industry and year with industry FE; firm and year with firm FE; firm only in some panel columns); the clustering level tracks the FE structure but no explicit rationale is given.

RD inference uses robust bias-corrected estimates and confidence intervals from the rdrobust framework, described as adjusting the variance estimator; p-values from the corresponding z-statistics are reported in parentheses.

Manipulation is checked visually with histograms at two zoom levels and formally with the local polynomial density test across fixed and data-driven bandwidths, including the first policy year; a footnote replicates a prior paper's manipulation finding at a different cutoff.
observations.locator: Figure 4, Table 4 Panel A, footnote 17, Table IA-7

observations.statement: A balance table covers close to fifty preassignment variables in seven groups, reporting treated and control means, difference, p-value, an RD estimate with its p-value, and counts; lagged values are also compared to check for multi-year trends.

The few marginally imbalanced covariates are discussed individually: one is argued irrelevant because it does not predict the outcome in the full sample, another is attributed to outliers with a supporting appendix figure.

Parallel trends are assessed with event-time indicators in the panel regression (pre-period coefficients tested against zero), a raw mean plot in the Internet Appendix, and a staggered DiD coefficient plot with confidence bands.
RD results are shown side by side for three fixed bandwidths and a data-driven bandwidth with linear and quadratic polynomials within the main table.

Placebo thresholds at fixed increments across the vote-share distribution are tested with both univariate differences and RD estimates in one table, with the true cutoff highlighted; further placebo RD analyses are in the Internet Appendix.
observations.locator: Section 5.2, Table 12, Table IA-11, Figure IA-3

observations.statement: Concern about staggered treatment bias in two-way FE DiD is addressed by re-estimating with the imputation estimator; coefficients are plotted in the main text and tabulated in the Internet Appendix, with magnitudes compared to the standard panel.
The return event study is re-run after dropping 8-K filings that bundle other material items, with the excluded item codes named; an RD version is placed in the Internet Appendix.

The main treatment effect is triangulated across three estimators (OLS/Poisson ATE with FE and controls, sharp RD without controls, panel DiD with firm FE), and differences in magnitude between them are explained by kernel weighting.
Determinant regressions are repeated with firm FE replacing industry FE within the same table, with clustering changed accordingly.
A supplementary check uses SEC EDGAR full-text search to see whether treated firms mention the proxy advisor in filings, reported in the Internet Appendix as corroboration of the channel.

Heterogeneity is tested by interacting treatment with ex ante director voting support and with board agency proxies (committee tenure, classified board) in the ATE regression; expected signs are stated before results.

The credibility of the enforcement threat is tested directly: firms are split by ex post responsiveness and the likelihood of an against recommendation is compared in a two-by-two univariate panel and in interaction regressions.
The agency-conflict analysis is labelled preliminary and placed in an Additional Tests section, with the interpretation framed as pointing to a channel rather than establishing it.
Effects are expressed as percentage-point changes relative to the sample or panel mean; Poisson coefficients are exponentiated in footnotes to give proportional changes.
Magnitudes from the staggered DiD and the standard panel are compared side by side, and a null result in the event study is discussed as possibly due to limited sample size.

The introduction has a limitations paragraph: reliance on voluntary disclosure as a proxy for actual engagement (mitigated by legal liability for proxy statements) and the inability to speak to the optimal level of engagement.
The determinants analysis is explicitly described as descriptive and unable to identify causal drivers; the paper also notes it cannot answer whether the advisor creates or destroys value on net.

Figures include a conceptual diagram of information flows, a bar-and-line time trend of the outcomes, a survey response chart, histograms of the running variable, binned RD plots with confidence bands, and an event-time coefficient plot.
Three-level stars from two-tailed tests are used throughout; table notes restate the treatment definition, sample, FE and clustering and refer to the variable appendix.
The univariate determinants table sorts into quintiles and adds a column giving the share of the sample with nonmissing data for each variable.
Appendices provide a timeline of treatment and measurement windows and reproduced examples of actual disclosure text with SEC source URLs.

The introduction walks through every result in order and then gives several contribution paragraphs; no roadmap paragraph. Hypotheses come first, then data and measures, then a descriptive determinants section, then identification and results.

Design validation (density, balance) is given its own subsection and table titled validity of research design before the estimating equations are introduced; many supporting tables and figures are pushed to an Internet Appendix.

Placebo thresholds and the agency-conflict analysis are gathered in an Additional Tests section after the main results; some section cross-references in the text point to numbers that do not match the printed headings.
A code availability line at the end of the conclusion cites a Harvard Dataverse DOI; Stata's rdrobust package is named in table notes and a Python scrape is described for variable construction.
observations.quote: The replication code is available in the Harvard Dataverse

observations.statement: Data come from commercial databases (ISS Voting Analytics, CRSP, Compustat, IBES, Thomson 13-F, WRDS SEC Analytics), public SEC filings, a private file from the proxy advisor, and FOIA-obtained recommendations; no data access procedure beyond the sources is described.
For the return event study, low-priced stocks are dropped to omit potentially distressed firms, stated in a footnote and repeated in the table note.
Abnormal returns are compounded daily returns over short windows around the first 8-K disclosing the vote, minus the CRSP value-weighted index; 8-K dates are downloaded from WRDS and hand-checked.
The event-study regression controls for the running variable within the narrow band and is described as functionally similar to an RD design.

gaps: No explicit rationale for the two-way clustering levels beyond matching the FE structure.
No power discussion for the RD subsample apart from a passing remark on sample size in the event study.
No data availability statement for the proprietary ISS file or FOIA data; only code availability is given.
No multiple-testing adjustment discussed despite many outcomes and placebo thresholds.
No preregistration or ethics statement (not expected for archival data).

reading.note: Main text (pages 1 to 47) read fully; Appendices A to C (pages 48 to 52) and the reference list (pages 52 to 55) read in full since they are short. The Internet Appendix is not part of the text file and was not read.
